**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (338 words):**

In October 2018 the dollar on Bitfinex fell far enough below bank money for our monitor to flag it 3 days before the exchange's deposit freeze was reported, and about 6.5 months before regulators disclosed the loss behind it. Web price feeds and on-chain oracles miss signals like this because they average prices across exchanges as if every exchange used the same dollar; CoinMarketCap dropped Bitfinex from its bitcoin average by hand only in May 2019, about 7 months after our monitor first flagged it. Some exchanges quote stablecoin tokens, and others quote balances in their own ledger, which become bank money only through the exchange's banks. When that link breaks, the exchange's dollar drifts, and a feed reads the drift as a price move or blames the stablecoin. We tell the two apart by pricing the exchange's own dollar with the law of one price across exchanges and triangular arbitrage within one. Bitcoin has no peg, so its gap between the troubled exchange and a reference exchange whose banking still works measures the ledger's loss of value, and whatever remains of a stablecoin's dislocation belongs to the token. We accept the split only when an unrelated asset shows the same gap, the implied token price matches its direct price elsewhere, and the exchange's internal cross-rates hold. In banking cut-offs on three exchanges from 2017 to 2023, the exchange's dollar broke on Bitfinex and Binance.US but barely moved when Binance lost its sterling and euro rails. On Bitfinex it fell by up to 844 basis points, with bitcoin and ether agreeing to within 7.2 and cross-rates holding to within 8. On both exchanges it traded first at a discount, then at a premium, and recovered when the episode ended. A multi-exchange bitcoin index was off by 100 basis points or more for 2,826 hours, and dropping the exchange-hours our monitor flags removes 88% of them. For the March 2023 USD Coin run it instead blames the token for all but 6% of the dislocation. All findings are descriptive.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
